attribution.note: Zitron credits Ramp but states the figure as fact and builds on it. He adds 'over the last three years' himself, which goes beyond Ramp's 'not getting better'.

semantics.note: Keeps the Ramp qualifier, the 80%/1% figures and 'hasn't improved over three years'. It is a backward-looking observation.

contract.note: Reading the claim as a Ramp-sample estimate, with rounded figures, fits the caveat in his text. Scoring the three-year trend depends on how 'improvement' and Ramp's sampling changes are treated.

evidence.note: Post by Ramp's economist dated 2026-09-02. It supports the 80%/1% headline and the 'not getting better' direction, but gives no period and no three-year series.

reviews.rationale: Ramp's own statement backs the headline figure. The support condition also requires comparable Ramp observations showing no material decline over three years, and the packet has none. The source rules say an economist's quote cannot supply missing historical data. Nothing contradicts the claim, so the claim as a whole is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: An unqualified 'will' with no deadline ('at some point'). The draft drops 'by the very nature of connecting to AI models' from the stated cause. That is a minor loss, and the meaning still holds.

contract.note: The plain reading covers venture-backed API customers who run out of cash because of service economics, with enough breadth to count. Excluding isolated failures is fair to the speaker.

evidence.note: Harvey raised new money after the post. Access to capital is not proof of viable economics, and it does not refute a forecast with no deadline.
Character.ai filed for bankruptcy in October 2026, citing legal and regulatory causes. The packet does not show it belongs to the API-customer population or failed because it could not pay the labs.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was given, and nothing in the packet meets the early-resolution rule. There is no broad funding exhaustion tied to model costs, and no durable self-funding across the population. A single bankruptcy with other stated causes, and one new funding round, settle nothing.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: Keeps 'nobody', the Microsoft exception, the debt claim and the shrinking customer pool. 'Near-infinite' is hyperbole, but the underlying claim is firm.

contract.note: Reading 'near-infinite' as substantial continuing borrowing is fair. The speaker named no period, so the contract chose Q2 2026, yet 'keep buying' implies a sustained period. That means the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Meta's own Q2 2026 release reports slightly positive free cash flow after $31B of capex, alongside existing debt. It covers one quarter, is a company disclosure, does not isolate NVIDIA costs, and is not a sustained self-funding test.

reviews.rationale: Meta's near-breakeven free cash flow in one quarter neither shows that it needs heavy borrowing nor shows durable self-funding. The packet has no data for the other buyers, no separation of GPU costs, and no measure of buyers priced out. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: Keeps the necessary conditions (about 10x growth in three years, plus eventual profitability) and the $1T requirement. The draft softens 'will require' to 'would need', which is minor.

contract.note: Reading growth as revenue growth, with a 2029-09-08 deadline, is an ordinary reading. The contract flags the combined-versus-per-company question for the $1T figure.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own announcement of $122B in committed capital (March 2026). It does not show future payment performance, three-year growth, or total financing for either company.

reviews.rationale: The growth deadline (2029-09-08) falls after the evaluation date, the condition is not yet known, and no conclusive event has occurred. The forecast cannot be scored yet.
